content: Loxoprofen is classified as a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and belongs to the propionic acid derivatives group, which also includes other well-known drugs such as ibuprofen and naproxen. It is marketed in Brazil, Mexico, and Japan by the pharmaceutical company Sankyo under the trade name Loxonin, where it is available as its sodium salt form, loxoprofen sodium. In Argentina, it is sold under the trade name Oxeno. In these countries, loxoprofen is available for oral administration, and a transdermal preparation was approved for sale in Japan in January 2006. Loxoprofen is a prodrug, meaning it requires metabolic activation to exert its therapeutic effects. After oral administration, it is rapidly converted into its active metabolite, trans-alcohol, which reaches peak plasma concentrations within 30 to 50 minutes. The mechanism of action of loxoprofen, like most NSAIDs, involves non-selective inhibition of cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes. This inhibition reduces the synthesis of prostaglandins from arachidonic acid, which are mediators of inflammation, pain, and fever. Loxoprofen should not be used concurrently with second-generation quinolone antibiotics, such as ciprofloxacin and norfloxacin, as this combination can enhance the inhibition of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) activity, potentially leading to seizures. Additionally, loxoprofen may increase the plasma concentrations of certain drugs, including warfarin, methotrexate, sulfonylurea derivatives, and lithium salts. Therefore, caution is advised when administering loxoprofen to patients who are taking any of these medications to avoid potential drug interactions.
